title: Monthly revenue
body:
Return each month (formatted YYYY-MM) and its revenue rounded to 2 decimals, oldest month first.

Revenue means the sum of quantity × price from order_items joined to products, for orders with status = 'completed'.
solution:
select strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) as month, round(sum(oi.quantity * p.price), 2) as revenue
from orders o
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
where o.status = 'completed'
group by month
order by month;
hint: Join the three tables, filter completed orders, and group by strftime('%Y-%m', order_date).

title: Top five customers
body:
Return the name and revenue (rounded to 2) of the five customers with the highest revenue. Break ties by name.

Revenue means the sum of quantity × price from order_items joined to products, for orders with status = 'completed'.
solution:
select c.name, round(sum(oi.quantity * p.price), 2) as revenue
from customers c
join orders o on o.customer_id = c.customer_id
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
where o.status = 'completed'
group by c.customer_id, c.name
order by revenue desc, c.name
limit 5;
hint: Group by customer, order by revenue descending, then LIMIT 5.

title: Best seller in each category
body: For completed orders, find the product with the most units sold in each category. If two products tie, pick the lower product_id. Return category, name, units, sorted by category.
solution:
with u as (
  select p.category, p.product_id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) as units
  from order_items oi
  join orders o on o.order_id = oi.order_id
  join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
  where o.status = 'completed'
  group by p.product_id
), r as (
  select *, row_number() over (partition by category order by units desc, product_id) as rn from u
)
select category, name, units from r where rn = 1 order by category;
hint: Aggregate units per product in a CTE, then ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC, product_id) and keep row 1.

title: Revenue for every day
body:
Return one row for every day in June 2025 with columns day and revenue (rounded to 2). Days without orders must show 0.

Revenue means the sum of quantity × price from order_items joined to products, for orders with status = 'completed'.
solution:
with recursive days(d) as (
  select '2025-06-01'
  union all
  select date(d, '+1 day') from days where d < '2025-06-30'
), rev as (
  select o.order_date as d, sum(oi.quantity * p.price) as revenue
  from orders o
  join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
  join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
  where o.status = 'completed'
  group by o.order_date
)
select days.d as day, round(coalesce(rev.revenue, 0), 2) as revenue
from days left join rev on rev.d = days.d
order by day;
hint: Build a date spine with a recursive CTE, then LEFT JOIN daily revenue onto it and COALESCE missing days to 0.

title: Pivot statuses into columns
body: For orders placed in 2025, return one row per month (YYYY-MM) with three columns counting orders by status: completed, returned, cancelled. Oldest month first.
solution:
select strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) as month,
       sum(status = 'completed') as completed,
       sum(status = 'returned') as returned,
       sum(status = 'cancelled') as cancelled
from orders
where order_date >= '2025-01-01'
group by month
order by month;
hint: Conditional aggregation: in SQLite a comparison is 1 or 0, so SUM(status = 'completed') counts matches. SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) works everywhere.

title: Cumulative revenue share
body:
Rank customers by revenue (highest first, ties by name) and return name, revenue (rounded to 2), and cum_pct: the running share of total revenue in percent, rounded to 1. The last row should be 100.0.

Revenue means the sum of quantity × price from order_items joined to products, for orders with status = 'completed'.
solution:
with r as (
  select c.name, sum(oi.quantity * p.price) as revenue
  from customers c
  join orders o on o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
  join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
  where o.status = 'completed'
  group by c.customer_id, c.name
)
select name, round(revenue, 2) as revenue,
       round(100.0 * sum(revenue) over (order by revenue desc, name rows unbounded preceding)
             / sum(revenue) over (), 1) as cum_pct
from r
order by revenue desc, name;
hint: A running total is SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING); the grand total is SUM(x) OVER ().

title: Median order value by segment
body: An order's value is the sum of quantity × price over its items. For completed orders, return each customer segment and its median_value (rounded to 2), sorted by segment. SQLite has no MEDIAN function.
solution:
with v as (
  select c.segment, o.order_id, sum(oi.quantity * p.price) as value
  from orders o
  join customers c on c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
  join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
  where o.status = 'completed'
  group by o.order_id
), r as (
  select segment, value,
         row_number() over (partition by segment order by value) as rn,
         count(*) over (partition by segment) as n
  from v
)
select segment, round(avg(value), 2) as median_value
from r
where rn in ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
group by segment
order by segment;
hint: Number the values within each segment and count them. The median is the middle row, or the average of the two middle rows: rn IN ((n+1)/2, (n+2)/2) with integer division.

title: Signup cohort conversion
body: Group customers by signup month (cohort, YYYY-MM). For each cohort return customers, converted (customers with a completed order within 90 days of signing up) and pct (converted as a percent, rounded to 1). Oldest cohort first.
solution:
with f as (
  select c.customer_id, strftime('%Y-%m', c.signup_date) as cohort,
         exists (select 1 from orders o
                 where o.customer_id = c.customer_id and o.status = 'completed'
                   and julianday(o.order_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) <= 90) as converted
  from customers c
)
select cohort, count(*) as customers, sum(converted) as converted,
       round(100.0 * sum(converted) / count(*), 1) as pct
from f
group by cohort
order by cohort;
hint: Flag each customer first (an EXISTS subquery returns 1 or 0), then aggregate the flags by cohort.

title: Ordered conversion funnel
body: Using events, count distinct users at each funnel step. A user counts as viewed if they have any view; as carted only if they added to cart after their first view; as purchased only if they purchased after their first qualifying add-to-cart. Return one row: viewed, carted, purchased.
solution:
with v as (
  select user_id, min(event_time) as t from events where event_type = 'view' group by user_id
), c as (
  select e.user_id, min(e.event_time) as t
  from events e join v on v.user_id = e.user_id
  where e.event_type = 'add_to_cart' and e.event_time > v.t
  group by e.user_id
), p as (
  select e.user_id, min(e.event_time) as t
  from events e join c on c.user_id = e.user_id
  where e.event_type = 'purchase' and e.event_time > c.t
  group by e.user_id
)
select (select count(*) from v) as viewed,
       (select count(*) from c) as carted,
       (select count(*) from p) as purchased;
hint: Chain CTEs: first view per user, then first cart after that view, then first purchase after that cart.

title: Data quality: missing values
body: Profile the customers table. Return one row with total_rows, null_city (rows with no city) and null_segment.
solution:
select count(*) as total_rows,
       sum(city is null) as null_city,
       sum(segment is null) as null_segment
from customers;
hint: COUNT(*) counts rows; SUM(col IS NULL) counts missing values. COUNT(col) counts non-missing ones.

title: Spot duplicate loads
body: raw_orders is a landing table: some orders were ingested more than once. Return total_rows, distinct_orders (distinct order_ids) and exact_duplicates (rows that are identical copies of another row in every column).
solution:
select count(*) as total_rows,
       count(distinct order_id) as distinct_orders,
       count(*) - (select count(*) from (select distinct * from raw_orders)) as exact_duplicates
from raw_orders;
hint: SELECT DISTINCT * collapses identical rows; compare its count with the total.

title: Create a reporting view
body:
Create a view v_order_totals with one row per order: order_id, order_date, status and order_total (sum of quantity × price, rounded to 2). Items whose product is missing are left out.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT * FROM v_order_totals ORDER BY order_id and compares the result with the expected state.
solution:
create view v_order_totals as
select o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status, round(sum(oi.quantity * p.price), 2) as order_total
from orders o
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
group by o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status;
hint: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT .... An inner join to products drops items with unknown products.
check: SELECT * FROM v_order_totals ORDER BY order_id

title: Create and load a staging table
body:
Create a table stg_gear with columns product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL and price REAL with a check that price is positive. Load it with every product in the Gear category.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT product_id, name, price FROM stg_gear ORDER BY product_id and compares the result with the expected state.
hint: CREATE TABLE with a CHECK (price > 0) constraint, then INSERT INTO ... SELECT ....
check: SELECT product_id, name, price FROM stg_gear ORDER BY product_id

title: Keep the latest version
body: In raw_orders, an order can appear several times; the row with the latest ingested_at is the current version. Return the current version of every order: order_id, status, ingested_at, sorted by order_id.
hint: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY ingested_at DESC), keep rn = 1.

title: Referential integrity check
body: Find rows in order_items whose product_id doesn't exist in products. Return order_id and product_id, sorted by order_id.
solution:
select oi.order_id, oi.product_id
from order_items oi
left join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
where p.product_id is null
order by oi.order_id;
hint: An anti-join: LEFT JOIN and keep rows where the right side is NULL (or use NOT EXISTS).

title: Upsert from a staging table
body:
product_updates holds new prices for some products and two brand-new products. Apply it to products in one statement: update existing rows and insert new ones.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY product_id and compares the result with the expected state.
solution:
insert into products (product_id, name, category, price)
select product_id, name, category, price from product_updates where true
on conflict(product_id) do update set
  name = excluded.name,
  category = excluded.category,
  price = excluded.price;
hint: INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col. SQLite needs a WHERE clause (even WHERE true) on the SELECT so it can parse the ON CONFLICT.
check: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY product_id

title: Incremental load with a watermark
body:
fact_orders(order_id, order_date, amount) holds completed orders up to the latest order_date already loaded. Load only the newer completed orders, with amount = sum of quantity × price rounded to 2. Use the table's own maximum date as the watermark, so running your SQL twice never adds duplicates.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT count(*), round(sum(amount), 2), max(order_date) FROM fact_orders and compares the result with the expected state.
solution:
insert into fact_orders (order_id, order_date, amount)
select o.order_id, o.order_date, round(sum(oi.quantity * p.price), 2)
from orders o
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
where o.status = 'completed'
  and o.order_date > (select max(order_date) from fact_orders)
group by o.order_id, o.order_date;
hint: Filter with order_date > (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM fact_orders) inside an INSERT ... SELECT.
check: SELECT count(*), round(sum(amount), 2), max(order_date) FROM fact_orders

title: Parse JSON payloads
body: raw_events_json.payload holds JSON like {"user": {"id": 3, "tier": "gold"}, "event": "view", "device": "ios", "cart_value": null}. Return each device, the number of events, and avg_cart_value (average of non-null cart values, rounded to 2), sorted by device.
solution:
select json_extract(payload, '$.device') as device,
       count(*) as events,
       round(avg(json_extract(payload, '$.cart_value')), 2) as avg_cart_value
from raw_events_json
group by device
order by device;
hint: json_extract(payload, '$.device') pulls a field out. AVG ignores NULLs.

title: Point-in-time join to an SCD2 dimension
body: dim_customer is a type-2 slowly changing dimension: each row is valid from valid_from (inclusive) to valid_to (exclusive). For completed orders placed in 2025, return revenue by the city the customer lived in when they ordered. Show missing cities as Unknown. Columns city, revenue (rounded to 2), highest revenue first.
solution:
select coalesce(d.city, 'Unknown') as city, round(sum(oi.quantity * p.price), 2) as revenue
from orders o
join dim_customer d on d.customer_id = o.customer_id
                   and o.order_date >= d.valid_from and o.order_date < d.valid_to
join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.order_id
join products p on p.product_id = oi.product_id
where o.status = 'completed' and o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'
group by coalesce(d.city, 'Unknown')
order by revenue desc;
hint: Join on the customer id and the date range: order_date >= valid_from AND order_date < valid_to.

title: Apply an SCD type 2 load
body:
customer_updates holds today's customer records (updated_on = 2025-07-01). Apply them to dim_customer as SCD type 2:

  • If a customer's city or segment changed, close their current row (valid_to = updated_on, is_current = 0) and insert a new current row (valid_from = updated_on, valid_to = '9999-12-31', is_current = 1).
  • If nothing changed, leave them alone.
  • New customers get a current row.

Cities can be NULL, so compare with IS NOT, not <>. customer_key fills itself in.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT customer_id, city, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current FROM dim_customer ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from and compares the result with the expected state.
solution:
-- 1. close current rows that changed
update dim_customer
set valid_to = (select u.updated_on from customer_updates u where u.customer_id = dim_customer.customer_id),
    is_current = 0
where is_current = 1
  and exists (select 1 from customer_updates u
              where u.customer_id = dim_customer.customer_id
                and (u.city is not dim_customer.city or u.segment is not dim_customer.segment));

-- 2. insert a current row for every changed or new customer
insert into dim_customer (customer_id, city, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
select u.customer_id, u.city, u.segment, u.updated_on, '9999-12-31', 1
from customer_updates u
where not exists (select 1 from dim_customer d where d.customer_id = u.customer_id and d.is_current = 1);
hint: Two statements: an UPDATE that closes changed current rows, then an INSERT ... SELECT for every update that no longer has a current row (changed or brand new).
check: SELECT customer_id, city, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current FROM dim_customer ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from

title: Downtime episodes (gaps and islands)
body: machine_status has one reading per machine every 10 minutes. A downtime episode is a run of consecutive DOWN readings. Return machine_id, started (first DOWN reading), ended (last DOWN reading), readings and minutes (readings × 10), sorted by machine and start.
solution:
with s as (
  select machine_id, ts, status,
         row_number() over (partition by machine_id order by ts)
       - row_number() over (partition by machine_id, status order by ts) as grp
  from machine_status
)
select machine_id, min(ts) as started, max(ts) as ended, count(*) as readings, count(*) * 10 as minutes
from s
where status = 'DOWN'
group by machine_id, grp
order by machine_id, started;
hint: The classic trick: the difference between a row number over all readings and a row number within each status is constant inside a run. Group by it.

title: Sessionise clickstream events
body: Split each user's events into sessions: a new session starts at a user's first event and whenever more than 30 minutes pass since their previous event. Return user_id, session_no (1, 2, … per user), session_start, session_end and events, sorted by user and session.
solution:
with e as (
  select user_id, event_time,
         case when lag(event_time) over (partition by user_id order by event_time) is null
                or (julianday(event_time)
                    - julianday(lag(event_time) over (partition by user_id order by event_time))) * 1440 > 30
              then 1 else 0 end as new_session
  from events
), s as (
  select *, sum(new_session) over (partition by user_id order by event_time rows unbounded preceding) as session_no
  from e
)
select user_id, session_no, min(event_time) as session_start, max(event_time) as session_end, count(*) as events
from s
group by user_id, session_no
order by user_id, session_no;
hint: Flag a new session with LAG() and a gap test (julianday difference × 1440 gives minutes), then a running SUM of the flags numbers the sessions.

title: Remove exact duplicates in place
body:
Delete exact duplicate rows from raw_orders, keeping one copy of each. Rows that differ in any column (for example a later ingested_at) must stay.

This task changes the database. After your SQL runs, the checker runs SELECT * FROM raw_orders ORDER BY order_id, ingested_at, status and compares the result with the expected state.
hint: Every SQLite table has a hidden rowid. Keep the smallest rowid in each group of identical rows and delete the rest.
check: SELECT * FROM raw_orders ORDER BY order_id, ingested_at, status
